turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Every developer wants to know how people use their app. But many users worry about privacy. How do you balance that?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I think the key is privacy-first analytics. You collect only the data you really need to improve the app, and nothing that identifies a person.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: What does that look like in practice?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: For example, I want to know how many people use a new feature. I don't need their name, email or location for that. I just count events, like 'export button tapped,' and look at the totals.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. Event tracking can be done without building a profile of each user. Many traditional analytics tools collect much more telemetry than developers actually look at. That's a risk, and it doesn't help anyone.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Does Apple have rules about this?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes. If you track users across other companies' apps or websites, you have to ask permission through App Tracking Transparency. And every app must show a privacy label on the App Store, explaining what data it collects.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Do users really read those labels?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: More and more do. A short, honest label can actually become a selling point. Users trust apps that clearly respect their privacy. And trust is very hard to win back once you lose it.
